Name: validation_selection_curse
Title: I Can't Believe It's Not Better: Quantifying the Validation Selection Curse in Applied Deep Learning
Short Hypothesis: Validation-based model selection in applied deep learning systematically overestimates deployment performance, and this 'selection curse' grows with the number of candidate models/checkpoints and with the severity of distribution shift between validation and deployment. A controlled empirical study is needed because existing theoretical work on adaptive data analysis does not characterize the practical DL pipeline, and a simple train/test split cannot expose the curse since the deployment distribution is not observed. We test this with synthetic and natural shifts, and propose a parameter-free worst-case multi-split selection protocol as a mitigation.
Related Work: Our proposal builds on and distinguishes from several lines of work. Adaptive data analysis (Dwork et al., 2015; Blum & Hardt, 2015) theoretically shows that reusing a dataset for multiple selections can overfit, but focuses on simple settings and asymptotic bounds, not on the practical pipeline of many architectures, hyperparameters, and checkpoints. The statistical winner's curse has been documented in model selection, but not systematically quantified for deep learning deployment under distribution shift. Model soups (Wortsman et al., 2022) show that weight averaging improves robustness, but our work targets the selection protocol itself rather than weight averaging. Recent empirical work (e.g., Szyc et al., 2024) shows that averaged metrics hide per-class failures, but does not address selection bias. Our contribution is a controlled, reproducible study of validation-based selection in realistic applied DL pipelines, with a simple and actionable mitigation.
Abstract: Deep learning models are routinely selected by maximizing performance on a validation set. Yet in applied settings, models that score best on validation often disappoint at deployment. We propose a systematic empirical study of this 'validation selection curse': the tendency for validation-based model selection to systematically overestimate deployment performance and to select models that are less robust to distribution shift. We hypothesize that the curse grows with the number of candidate models, checkpoints, and the severity of shift between validation and deployment distributions. We test this in controlled settings using standard image and tabular benchmarks with synthetic and natural distribution shifts, training many architectures and hyperparameter configurations. We measure the selection gap (validation minus deployment performance) and selection regret (deployment performance relative to an oracle) as a function of candidate count, validation set size, and shift severity. We also study checkpoint selection within a single training run, showing that the best validation checkpoint is often worse than the median or last checkpoint on deployment. Finally, we propose and evaluate simple, parameter-free mitigations: worst-case validation across multiple random splits, variance-penalized selection, and deferred selection on a small deployment-probe set. Our results provide a cautionary tale for applied DL: validation performance is not a reliable proxy for deployment performance, and standard selection practices may be actively harmful. We release code and a diagnostic toolkit so practitioners can quantify the selection curse in their own pipelines.
Experiments: 1. Controlled selection-curse study: Use CIFAR-10 as the source domain and CIFAR-10-C (corruption shift) plus a resized STL-10 domain shift as deployment sets; also use a tabular benchmark with synthetic covariate shift. Train ResNet-18/34, ViT-Small, and MLP models over a grid of learning rate, weight decay, dropout, batch size, and augmentation, yielding up to 100 candidate models. For each candidate count K in {1, 5, 10, 25, 50, 100}, sample K models, select the one with highest validation accuracy, and evaluate on deployment. Repeat 20 times with different seeds and validation splits. Metrics: deployment accuracy/AUC, validation-deployment gap, selection regret (oracle deployment accuracy minus selected deployment accuracy), and worst-class accuracy. Hypothesis: gap and regret increase with K and shift severity; for large K, selected deployment performance may be no better than a randomly chosen model. 2. Checkpoint selection study: Train a single ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10 with 5 seeds, recording validation and deployment performance at every epoch. Compare selection strategies: best validation epoch, last epoch, median validation epoch, average validation across seeds, and smoothed validation (rolling average). Measure deployment performance and validation-deployment gap. Hypothesis: the best validation checkpoint has higher validation but lower deployment performance than median or smoothed checkpoints. 3. Mitigation evaluation: Compare standard selection (argmax V) against (a) multi-split worst-case: split validation into S=5 or 10 random subsets, select argmax min_s V_s; (b) variance-penalized: select argmax (mean_s V_s - lambda * std_s V_s) for lambda in {0.1, 0.5, 1.0}; (c) deferred selection: select top-K by validation, then evaluate on a small deployment-probe set (e.g., 500 samples) and pick the best. Report deployment accuracy, worst-class accuracy, expected calibration error, selection regret, and paired bootstrap significance tests. 4. Ablations: Vary validation set size, candidate count, shift severity, and model family; verify whether mitigations consistently help. Include a real-world case study using a medical tabular dataset with a temporal split to show the effect outside synthetic shifts. All experiments use small-scale models and datasets feasible in an academic lab.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The phenomenon is statistically well-known, so the main risk is being perceived as incremental; we mitigate this by focusing on the practical DL pipeline (many candidates, checkpoints, and shifts) and by providing an actionable, parameter-free mitigation plus a diagnostic toolkit. Simulated shifts may not fully capture real deployment; we use multiple shift types and a real-world temporal-split case study to increase validity. The effect may be small when validation and deployment distributions are highly correlated; we vary shift severity to identify the regime where it matters. Multi-split worst-case selection may be too conservative and reduce validation performance; we report the trade-off. Deferred selection assumes access to a small deployment-probe set, which may not be available in practice; we frame it as a pilot deployment and discuss its limitations. Computational cost is kept manageable by using small datasets and a limited hyperparameter grid, but training many candidates is still expensive; we use shared seeds and early stopping to control budget.
